blocks.text: Drought

Recently, Haverhill's water supply [entered the status Critical Drought (timestamp 29:17)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). It's difficult to understand what this means and why it's happening, and much of the information is only available through recorded meetings that are time consuming to review. This page provides a summary of information that's been shared and an analysis of concerns that have been raised to make it easier for people to understand what's going on.

This site is not affiliated with the city of Haverhill and nothing here should be regarded as an official statement by the city. Members of the city were consulted in the development of this page, any information they provide which isn't publicly available has been made available where it is relevant.

Haverhill defines a drought based on the [level of Kenoza Lake](https://ecode360.com/31349794), but it's important to understand that this is a proxy which combines the demand of our city with water sources available to us. Steps taken to artificially increase this level which do not either reduce demand or increase supply therefore solve the symptom rather than the problem.
Water Sources

Our water is [primarily replenished through rainfall](https://www.haverhillma.gov/living-here/waterwastewater-services/water-supplydrought-information/), which runs into Crystal Lake, Millvale Reservoir and Kenoza Lake. In the spring, snow melt also runs into these water supplies, making up another significant source.
Precipitation

Over the last several years, our rainfall has mostly been [below average](https://xmacis.rcc-acis.org/), and unfortunately this means the water supply has not kept pace with our consumption. As a result, each year we've had to draw on our reserves and these are diminishing. [Climate change strongly affects precipitation](https://www.c2es.org/content/extreme-precipitation-and-climate-change/), which means this problem is unlikely to go away any time soon.

The pumps connected to these bodies of water have limited capacity, and with too much rainfall they have the potential to overflow. This is particularly true of Millvale Reservoir, which is [relatively small and has a large watershed (timestamp 22:43)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-meeting-march-30-2026).

When snow melts in the Spring, this runs into our water supply as much as possible. This helps replenish Kenoza in the Spring, but if it melts too quickly it's subject to the same limitations as heavy rainfall. Snowfall melted quickly this year, which [limited our ability to capture it in our water supply (timestamp 35:22)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026).
Beaver Dams

[Residents have noticed that more beaver dams have been constructed recently (timestamp 1:30:00)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-october-6-2026), expressing concerns that this is preventing water from getting into our water supply. [These are protected](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/addressing-property-damage-from-beaver-activity) because of their [ecological benefits](https://www.epa.gov/sciencematters/how-do-beaver-dams-affect-water-quality), though, so removing them could be complicated.

It should also be noted that these dams create new pools, but they probably don't limit the supply all that much. The drought is a result of decreased water coming into the system, removing these dams would only have a one time increase to what's in the lake. One way to think about this is that the water behind a beaver dam is like a full tub; if you pour a bottle of water into the tub then a bottle's worth of water would overflow.
New Hampshire Drawdown

[New Hampshire reduces lake levels annually](https://www.des.nh.gov/news-and-media/state-announces-its-2026-fall-drawdown-lakes), and [some have suggested some of Salem's drawdown could be diverted into our water supply (timestamp 1:23:10)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026). There are [regulatory restrictions on moving water from other bodies of water into our water supply, though, ones which would be complicated to circumvent (timestamp 1:28:10)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026). [Transporting that water would also be extremely expensive (timestamp 1:27:30)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026), significantly more than other options available to the city to supplement our water supply.
Consumption

Haverhill consumes approximately 6 million gallons of water a day. In dry years, this goes up significantly during the summer, when we had all of that rainfall in 2023 [we used 204 million gallons less than 2022 (timestamp 44:19)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) which was considerably more dry.
Industry/Commercial Use

Haverhill sees [heavy industry use (timestamp 1:18:41)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026), in 2025 [51.06% of our total water usage](ref:cy25-water-usage.xlsx) was from that sector. It was [implied in the September drought update that voluntary conservation has not had a significant impact (timestamp 1:19:14)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) and [the city is currently investigating tiered pricing to create a stronger incentive for these businesses (timestamp 1:32:20)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026).

Car washes are an extremely visible water consumer, many of which justify operation during droughts because of how much water they're able to reclaim. Much of the information out there, though, is published by car washes which obviously have a vested interest in remaining open. The EPA published [a guide in 2023](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-11/ws-commercial-bmp-watersenseatwork_section5.4_vehiclewashes.pdf) which includes some numbers:
Type | Per Vehicle Use | Use After Reclamation
Conveyor Systems | 65.8 gallons | 30.0 gallons
In-Bay Automatic | 85.3 gallons | 43.3 gallons
Self-Service | 15.0 gallons | 15.0 gallons

As you can see, reclamation systems do save a lot of water, but even with those in place they still use significantly more than self service washing. In that situation, reclamation isn't possible because of activities like changing oil in the bays which would damage the filters. It's possible that the equipment available for self service translates to significant conservation, but it's difficult to compare to home washing because most sources estimating that usage are biased.

Another visible commercial use is golf courses, which are explicitly exempted since it is considered a core function of their business. According to the water department, though, [most golf courses get their water elsewhere (timestamp 1:17:40)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). Golf courses aren't particularly forthcoming on their watering practices, though, and depending on what they're doing it could still impact drought conditions.
Well Usage

Well usage can potentially [have an impact on the available water supply](https://pubs.usgs.gov/circ/1376/pdf/circ1376_barlow_report_508.pdf), depending on a combination of geological factors and the location of the well. As a rule of thumb, if a well is within the watershed of one of the city's water supplies, pumping from it probably reduces what will flow into that supply.

When wells pump, they create something called a cone of depression around them where water begins flowing towards the well. If this cone becomes large enough to interact with a nearby stream, the flow of that stream will be reduced to supply water to the well. The size of the cone depends heavily on geologic factors and how much is being pumped from the well. There doesn't seem to be publicly available data on this information for our areas, but the geologically similar Ipswich River basin has been [heavily studied](https://pubs.usgs.gov/wri/wri004029/whole_report.pdf). It was found that well pumping in that area had a significant effect on flow rates of streams and rivers.

The location of the well matters greatly. Since all of our water supplies are north of the Merrimack, it's incredibly unlikely that wells south of the river would impact them. On the other hand, [Crystal Lake is spring fed (timestamp 19:23)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-meeting-march-30-2026) so if it's in that watershed it's extremely likely to be influencing drought conditions.
New Apartment Buildings

There have been concerns expressed about new apartment buildings bringing more people into the city than our water supply can handle. In the drought update, the city provided some data on [how much water some of these new buildings use (timestamp 44:26)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). By only measuring the usage of some of those developments, though, it's difficult to see if that information is comprehensive enough to fully represent the added strain this represents.

It's possible to get a closer approximation of new apartment usage by combining [population information from the census](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-total-cities-and-towns.html) with general usage statistics. There were 1040 new residents added to the city in the last five years (difference between highest and lowest population years, 68,416 - 67,376), and each of these use approximately [51 gallons a day](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/public-water-supply-tools-resources-performance-standards). This translates to 39,780 gallons (1040 * 51 gallons), which is 0.884% of our overall usage (39,780 gallons / 6,000,000 gallons).
This calculation has some degree of error, but these factors go in both directions and hopefully balance each other:
The 2020 decennial census resulted in an upward adjustment of the population, making it difficult to use earlier numbers to exclude apartments constructed prior to that year.
Some of the new residents included in this calculation may have moved into a more traditional home.
Residents in apartment buildings do not have lawns, so outdoor water use is extremely minimal.

Older homes use substantially more water than new construction; for example, our average of 51 is significantly higher than the [Boston average of 38.1](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/public-water-supply-tools-resources-performance-standards).
City Response

The city has known for a while that our water supply is vulnerable, and earlier this year they [acquired property (timestamp 13:06)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026) to allow us to pull water from the Merrimack River. This project will [take about two years to complete (timestamp 42:48)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026), so they are working on building [a connection to Methuen's water supply (timestamp 38:45)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) as a precaution if ours gets too low.
Merrimack River

The city is building a [Ranney Collector Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranney_collector) to collect from the groundwater beneath the Merrimack. This is estimated to provide up to [6-7 million gallons a day (timestamp 43:49)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026), effectively doubling our available water supply. This project [will cost around $26 million (timestamp 24:00)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026).

[309 E Broadway was acquired for $1.8 million (timestamp 30:01)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026) and has been going full speed ahead since July. The geologic properties beneath the river make this location [uniquely suited for collection (timestamp 15:11)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026), but obtaining it was somewhat challenging. The owner was not willing to sell the portion of land the city needed for this project, and on March 10th City Council [pushed back on the use of eminent domain (timestamp 39:00)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-march-10-2026). The city was then able to negotiate a more friendly taking of the full property which was [approved by City Council on June 2nd (timestamp 50:40)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026). It should also be noted that [this project dates back to 2012 (timestamp 26:45)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026), when the property was originally identified and a loan order approved by the council.

There may be concerns about the [sewage recently discharged into the river](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/sewer-force-main-break-in-haverhill-frequently-asked-questions) becoming our drinking water, as well as the landfill and paper mill being upriver of that site, but the [water is undergoing extensive testing to ensure that it is safe (timestamp 22:04)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026). Additionally, the layers of sediment it must pass through [act as a natural filter (timestamp 27:54)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026), and water actually reaching collection will [take decades (timestamp 23:15)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026) to pass through these layers.
Methuen

As mentioned earlier, we will soon have the ability to obtain water from Methuen. This will ensure that if decreased rainfall occurs for the next couple years, demand of the city will continue to be met. This will be [more expensive than using our own supply (timestamp 58:30)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026), though, although the exact impact on water rates has not been provided.

[The pipe for this connection is already mostly built (timestamp 57:50)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). The bigger issue revealed in that meeting, though, is that there is a [water chemistry problem between the two cities treatment methods (timestamp 38:55)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). Methuen is going to change their treatment process to match Haverhill's, something they've been planning to do for a while, which is estimated to be approved by the end of October.
Ordinance Changes

On October 6th, Haverhill approved [many revisions to the water use ordinance (timestamp 41:29)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-october-6-2026) to reduce resident usage during drought conditions. These include increased fines for violations such as lawn irrigation and new requirements for new and upgraded irrigation systems. These changes were [originally discussed on March 30th](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-meeting-march-30-2026), and several provisions were removed from those discussed. Most significantly, this included any restrictions for well users and irrigation restrictions during non-drought conditions.
Tiered Rates

City Council ordered the water department to [investigate tiered rates in mid-September (timestamp 1:32:20)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) during the drought update. These will hopefully curtail industry/commercial usage, but if they don't they will at least offset the costs associated with pulling water from Methuen or building the Ranney Collector Well. These could be implemented immediately once that investigation is complete, although no further update has been provided on this change.

blocks.text: Haverhill Drought

Recently, Haverhill's water supply [entered the status Critical Drought (timestamp 29:17)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). It's difficult to understand what this means and why it's happening, and much of the information is only available through recorded meetings that are time consuming to review. This page provides a summary of information that's been shared and an analysis of concerns that have been raised to make it easier for people to understand what's going on.

This site is not affiliated with the city of Haverhill and nothing here should be regarded as an official statement by the city. Members of the city were consulted in the development of this page, any information they provide which isn't publicly available has been made available where it is relevant.

Haverhill defines a drought based on the [level of Kenoza Lake](https://ecode360.com/31349794), but it's important to understand that this is a proxy which combines the demand of our city with water sources available to us. Steps taken to artificially increase this level which do not either reduce demand or increase supply therefore solve the symptom rather than the problem.
Water Sources

Our water is [primarily replenished through rainfall](https://www.haverhillma.gov/living-here/waterwastewater-services/water-supplydrought-information/), which runs into Crystal Lake, Millvale Reservoir and Kenoza Lake. In the spring, snow melt also runs into these water supplies, making up another significant source.
Precipitation

Over the last several years, our rainfall has mostly been [below average](https://xmacis.rcc-acis.org/), and unfortunately this means the water supply has not kept pace with our consumption. As a result, each year we've had to draw on our reserves and these are diminishing. [Climate change strongly affects precipitation](https://www.c2es.org/content/extreme-precipitation-and-climate-change/), which means this problem is unlikely to go away any time soon.

The pumps connected to these bodies of water have limited capacity, and with too much rainfall they have the potential to overflow. This is particularly true of Millvale Reservoir, which is [relatively small and has a large watershed (timestamp 22:43)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-meeting-march-30-2026).

When snow melts in the Spring, this runs into our water supply as much as possible. This helps replenish Kenoza in the Spring, but if it melts too quickly it's subject to the same limitations as heavy rainfall. Snowfall melted quickly this year, which [limited our ability to capture it in our water supply (timestamp 35:22)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026).
Beaver Dams

[Residents have noticed that more beaver dams have been constructed recently (timestamp 1:30:00)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-october-6-2026), expressing concerns that this is preventing water from getting into our water supply. [These are protected](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/addressing-property-damage-from-beaver-activity) because of their [ecological benefits](https://www.epa.gov/sciencematters/how-do-beaver-dams-affect-water-quality), though, so removing them could be complicated.

It should also be noted that these dams create new pools, but they probably don't limit the supply all that much. The drought is a result of decreased water coming into the system, removing these dams would only have a one time increase to what's in the lake. One way to think about this is that the water behind a beaver dam is like a full tub; if you pour a bottle of water into the tub then a bottle's worth of water would overflow.
New Hampshire Drawdown

[New Hampshire reduces lake levels annually](https://www.des.nh.gov/news-and-media/state-announces-its-2026-fall-drawdown-lakes), and [some have suggested some of Salem's drawdown could be diverted into our water supply (timestamp 1:23:10)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026). There are [regulatory restrictions on moving water from other bodies of water into our water supply, though, ones which would be complicated to circumvent (timestamp 1:28:10)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026). [Transporting that water would also be extremely expensive (timestamp 1:27:30)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026), significantly more than other options available to the city to supplement our water supply.
Consumption

Haverhill consumes approximately 6 million gallons of water a day. In dry years, this goes up significantly during the summer, when we had all of that rainfall in 2023 [we used 204 million gallons less than 2022 (timestamp 44:19)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) which was considerably more dry.
Industry/Commercial Use

Haverhill sees [heavy industry use (timestamp 1:18:41)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026), in 2025 [51.06% of our total water usage](ref:cy25-water-usage.xlsx) was from that sector. It was [implied in the September drought update that voluntary conservation has not had a significant impact (timestamp 1:19:14)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) and [the city is currently investigating tiered pricing to create a stronger incentive for these businesses (timestamp 1:32:20)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026).

Car washes are an extremely visible water consumer, many of which justify operation during droughts because of how much water they're able to reclaim. Much of the information out there, though, is published by car washes which obviously have a vested interest in remaining open. Type | Per Vehicle Use | Use After Reclamation
Conveyor Systems | 65.8 gallons | 30.0 gallons
In-Bay Automatic | 85.3 gallons | 43.3 gallons
Self-Service | 15.0 gallons | 15.0 gallons

In that situation, reclamation isn't possible because of activities like changing oil in the bays which would damage the filters. It's possible that the equipment available for self service translates to significant conservation, but it's difficult to compare to home washing because most sources estimating that usage are biased.

There have been concerns expressed about new apartment buildings bringing more people into the city than our water supply can handle. In the drought update, the city provided some data on [how much water some of these new buildings use (timestamp 44:26)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026). This translates to 39,780 gallons (1040 * 51 gallons), which is 0.884% of our overall usage (39,780 gallons / 6,000,000 gallons).
This calculation has some degree of error, but these factors go in both directions and hopefully balance each other:
The 2020 decennial census resulted in an upward adjustment of the population, making it difficult to use earlier numbers to exclude apartments constructed prior to that year.
Some of the new residents included in this calculation may have moved into a more traditional home.
Residents in apartment buildings do not have lawns, so outdoor water use is extremely minimal.

Older homes use substantially more water than new construction; for example, our average of 51 is significantly higher than the [Boston average of 38.1](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/public-water-supply-tools-resources-performance-standards).

The city has known for a while that our water supply is vulnerable, and earlier this year they [acquired property (timestamp 13:06)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026) to allow us to pull water from the Merrimack River. The city is building a [Radial Collector Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranney_collector) to collect from the groundwater beneath the Merrimack. It should also be noted that [this project dates back to 2012 (timestamp 26:45)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-june-2-2026), when the property was originally identified and a loan order approved by the council.

On November 17 the [city announced](https://www.haverhillma.gov/news/posts/haverhill-mayor-takes-proactive-steps-to-address-water-supply-emergency/) that, in addition to drawing from a test well they had set up as part of the radial collector well permitting process, they were seeking emergency approval to draw water directly from the Merrimack. This will involve extensive testing and approvals, but if they are able to clear those hurdles this will be pumped into Millvale Reservoir.

blocks.text: Haverhill Drought

Recently, Haverhill's water supply [entered the status Critical Drought (timestamp 29:17)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026) ([slide 13](https://media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/haverhillma-003-us/media/evpcyauo/26-sept-15-drought-emergency-powerpoint.pptx)). It's difficult to understand what this means and why it's happening, and much of the information is only available through recorded meetings that are time consuming to review. This page provides a summary of information that's been shared and an analysis of concerns that have been raised to make it easier for people to understand what's going on.

This site is not affiliated with the city of Haverhill and nothing here should be regarded as an official statement by the city. Members of the city were consulted in the development of this page, any information they provide which isn't publicly available has been made available where it is relevant.

Haverhill defines a drought based on the [level of Kenoza Lake](https://ecode360.com/52046353), but it's important to understand that this is a proxy which combines the demand of our city with water sources available to us. Steps taken to artificially increase this level which do not either reduce demand or increase supply therefore solve the symptom rather than the problem.
Water Sources

Our water is [primarily replenished through rainfall](https://www.haverhillma.gov/living-here/waterwastewater-services/water-supplydrought-information/), which runs into Crystal Lake, Millvale Reservoir and Kenoza Lake. In the spring, snow melt also runs into these water supplies, making up another significant source.
Precipitation

Over the last several years, our rainfall has mostly been [below average](https://xmacis.rcc-acis.org/), and unfortunately this means the water supply has not kept pace with our consumption. As a result, each year we've had to draw on our reserves and these are diminishing. [Climate change strongly affects precipitation](https://www.c2es.org/content/extreme-precipitation-and-climate-change/), which means this problem is unlikely to go away any time soon.

The pumps connected to these bodies of water have limited capacity, and with too much rainfall they have the potential to overflow. This is particularly true of Millvale Reservoir, which is [relatively small and has a large watershed (timestamp 22:43)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-meeting-march-30-2026).

When snow melts in the Spring, this runs into our water supply as much as possible. This helps replenish Kenoza in the Spring, but if it melts too quickly it's subject to the same limitations as heavy rainfall. Snowfall melted quickly this year, which [limited our ability to capture it in our water supply (timestamp 35:22)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-september-15-2026).
Beaver Dams

[Residents have noticed that more beaver dams have been constructed recently (timestamp 1:30:00)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-meeting-october-6-2026), expressing concerns that this is preventing water from getting into our water supply. [These are protected](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/addressing-property-damage-from-beaver-activity) because of their [ecological benefits](https://www.epa.gov/sciencematters/how-do-beaver-dams-affect-water-quality), though, so removing them could be complicated.

It should also be noted that these dams create new pools, but they probably don't limit the supply all that much. The drought is a result of decreased water coming into the system, removing these dams would only have a one time increase to what's in the lake. One way to think about this is that the water behind a beaver dam is like a full tub; if you pour a bottle of water into the tub then a bottle's worth of water would overflow.

[New Hampshire reduces lake levels annually](https://www.des.nh.gov/news-and-media/state-announces-its-2026-fall-drawdown-lakes), and [some have suggested some of Salem's drawdown could be diverted into our water supply (timestamp 1:23:10)](http://haverhillcommunitytv.org/video/haverhill-city-council-planning-development-committee-meeting-october-19-2026). Haverhill consumes approximately 6 million gallons of water a day. Type | Per Vehicle Use | Use After Reclamation
Conveyor Systems | 65.8 gallons | 30.0 gallons
In-Bay Automatic | 85.3 gallons | 43.3 gallons
Self-Service | 15.0 gallons | 15.0 gallons

As you can see, reclamation systems do save a lot of water, but even with those in place they still use significantly more than self service washing. In that situation, reclamation isn't possible because of activities like changing oil in the bays which would damage the filters. It's possible that the equipment available for self service translates to significant conservation, but it's difficult to compare to home washing because most sources estimating that usage are biased.

Another visible commercial use is golf courses, which are explicitly exempted since it is considered a core function of their business ([slide 14](https://media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/haverhillma-003-us/media/evpcyauo/26-sept-15-drought-emergency-powerpoint.pptx)). As a rule of thumb, if a well is within the watershed of one of the city's water supplies, pumping from it probably reduces what will flow into that supply.

When wells pump, they create something called a cone of depression around them where water begins flowing towards the well. If this cone becomes large enough to interact with a nearby stream, the flow of that stream will be reduced to supply water to the well. The size of the cone depends heavily on geologic factors and how much is being pumped from the well.
